title: Make it understandable, not easier
desc: Comprehensible input is not watered-down input. Five words before the lesson, cognates on the board, chunk the talk, show everything twice, and the two-minute test for whether they got it.

cues.text: This is Every Teacher, from EL Publishing. I'm Marcus, I teach biology. Elena is our EL specialist. Episode two. Last time you said the whole game is English in and English out, every day. Let's do the in. How do I make a biology lesson understandable to a student who is at level one or two?

The phrase in the research is comprehensible input. And I want to be clear about what it is not. It is not a simpler lesson. It is not the worksheet from two grades down. It's the same content, delivered so that a learner of English can get a foothold. Same rigor, more handholds.
Give me the handholds.

Five of them. First one happens before the lesson. Pick five words. Not twenty. Five. The ones that, if a student doesn't have them, the whole lesson falls apart. For photosynthesis that's probably sunlight, energy, carbon dioxide, oxygen, and glucose. Put them on the board before you start. Say each one. Have the students say each one. Picture next to each. That's three minutes, and it's the best three minutes of the period.
I used to do a vocabulary list of thirty words on Monday and test it Friday.
And the newcomer learned none of them, because thirty words with no context is noise. Five words, with a picture, used ten times in the next hour, those stick.
Handhold two?

Cognates. If your English learners speak Spanish, and in Mississippi most of them do, then a huge share of science and social studies vocabulary is already theirs. Energy, energía. Organism, organismo. Democracy, democracia. Write the Spanish next to the English on your word wall. You don't need to speak Spanish. You just need to show the student that the big scary word is a word they already own. There's a tool on the hub called Cognate Hunt. You paste in your reading and it marks the cognates. Takes thirty seconds.
Handhold three. I'm guessing this is where you tell me I talk too much.

You talk too much. Everybody talks too much. Here's the fix: chunk it. Talk for three or four minutes, then stop, and do something. Turn to a partner and say the word for this. Point to the part of the diagram I just described. Thumbs up if this is a plant cell. Then talk for another three or four minutes. A level one student can track three minutes of talk if there's a picture. Nobody tracks fifteen.
And I'm supposed to slow down.

Slow down, but don't get weird about it. Don't talk louder, don't talk like a robot. Just pause at the ends of sentences. Use the same word for the same thing: if you called it a cell membrane at the start, don't call it a plasma membrane ten minutes later without saying those are the same. Native speakers handle that switch automatically. A learner thinks it's a new thing.
That's a good one. I do that constantly. Handhold four.

Show it twice. Whatever you say, also show. Say it, and point. Say it, and the slide has the diagram. Say it, and write the key word on the board as you say it. Say it, and act it out if you can. Diffusion: you walk across the room and spread your arms out. Every time you give the same idea in two channels, the student who missed it in one channel catches it in the other.
I have a colleague who teaches world history and says, I can't draw a picture of the Treaty of Versailles.

No, but you can draw a timeline. You can show a map. You can show two faces and an arrow, with the words lost and gained. You can show the actual photograph. History is one of the most visual subjects there is; textbooks just hide it behind text. And for history specifically, graphic organizers do a lot of work: cause and effect boxes, a timeline, a compare chart with two columns. The structure carries the meaning when the words can't.
Last handhold.

Check in a way that doesn't require English to answer. Hold up one finger or two. Point to the answer on the diagram. Sort these four cards into two piles. Draw it. A level one student who can't say it can very often show it, and if you only check with questions that need a spoken sentence, you'll think they got nothing when they got most of it.

Let me try the two-minute version of this on you. Tomorrow I'm teaching the parts of a cell. I put five words on the board with pictures: nucleus, membrane, cytoplasm, mitochondria, and cell. I write núcleo and membrana next to them. I talk for four minutes, then they label a diagram with a partner. I talk for four more, then they sort cards into plant and animal. I check by having everyone point.

That's a great lesson. And notice: you didn't change the content. The level one student is doing the same cell as everybody else. The level four student is doing the same cell and also writing the sentence about what the mitochondria does. Same lesson, different size of output.
What do I stop worrying about this time?

Stop worrying about translation apps. Teachers either ban them or hand everything over to them. Neither works. Let a newcomer use one to look up a word. Don't let the whole lesson become a screen. The tool is a dictionary, not a teacher.
Next episode: getting them to talk. Which is the part I was most scared of. Every Teacher is from EL Publishing. Free, no login, at radan55 dot github dot io slash everyteacher.
